Comparative advantages and limitations of g-\( C_3N_4 \) relative to other photocatalytic nanomaterials

The development of nanophotocatalysts for cancer therapy has expanded beyond conventional metal-oxide semiconductors to include two-dimensional materials, carbon-based nanomaterials, metal-organic frameworks (MOFs), and other multifunctional nanoplatforms. Representative systems include \( TiO_2 \) and \( ZnO \), graphene oxide (GO), black phosphorus (BP), transition-metal dichalcogenides such as \( MoS_2 \), MXenes, and MOFs. These materials possess distinct optical, electronic, catalytic, and surface properties that can be advantageous for photodynamic, photothermal, chemodynamic, drug-delivery, or multimodal cancer therapy. Therefore, positioning g-\( C_3N_4 \) within this broader nanomaterial landscape is important for defining both its advantages and its current limitations.

chunks.text: Surface engineering provides a second level of control over the biological and photocatalytic properties of \( \mathrm{g}-\mathrm{C}_{3}\mathrm{N}_{4} \) [7]. Heteroatom doping and defect engineering can modify the electronic structure and increase visible-light utilization, whereas heterojunction construction and noble-metal decoration primarily aim to improve interfacial charge separation and suppress electron–hole recombination [25]. These modifications can consequently enhance ROS production and therapeutic activity. Surface functionalization, in contrast, is particularly important for biomedical performance because it can improve colloidal stability, cellular interactions, drug loading, and tumor-targeting capability. Thus, modifications that maximize photocatalytic activity do not necessarily provide the optimal biological profile, and the selection of a surface-engineering strategy should consider both catalytic efficiency and biological compatibility. Recent studies have explored a range of modification approaches, including heteroatom doping, heterojunction construction, noble-metal decoration, oxygen-vacancy engineering, and surface functionalization [75]. Photocatalytic mechanisms for cancer therapy

Reactive oxygen species generation

The photocatalytic activity of \( \mathrm{g}-\mathrm{C}_{3}\mathrm{N}_{4} \)-based nanomaterials is primarily associated with their ability to generate reactive oxygen species (ROS) under appropriate light irradiation [59]. Upon absorption of photons with energies exceeding the effective bandgap, electrons are promoted from the valence band (VB) to the conduction band (CB), leaving photogenerated holes in the VB. The subsequent generation, migration, separation, and interfacial transfer of these charge carriers determine both the quantity and chemical identity of the ROS produced at the nanomaterial–biological interface [60].

Importantly, the therapeutic consequences of ROS generation depend not only on the total ROS level but also on ROS identity, lifetime, diffusion range, and subcellular site of formation.

Overall, characterization should be regarded as an integrated analytical framework linking material structure and surface chemistry \(\rightarrow\) optical and charge-carrier behavior \(\rightarrow\) catalytic/ROS activity \(\rightarrow\) biological interaction \(\rightarrow\) therapeutic efficacy and biosafety. Such an approach is particularly important for g-\( C_3N_4 \)-based smart nanocatalysts, where apparently small changes in morphology, defects, surface functionalization, or interfacial architecture can substantially alter PDT, PTT, CDT, drug-delivery, and imaging performance. A comprehensive overview of the key characterization techniques for g-\( C_3N_4 \)-based nanomaterials, together with their relevance to cancer theranostics, is provided in Table 2.

Comparative advantages and limitations of g-\( C_3N_4 \) relative to other photocatalytic nanomaterials

g-\(C_{3}N_{4}\)-based nanozymes represent a distinct class of catalytic nanomaterials that mimic the functional behavior of natural enzymes while providing the physicochemical advantages of inorganic or polymeric nanostructures. Unlike conventional CDT, which is primarily based on Fenton or Fenton-like chemical conversion of \(H_{3}O_{2}\) into \(\cdot OH\), nanozyme-mediated therapy relies on enzyme-like catalytic activity, in which nanomaterials can catalytically participate in biochemical reactions without being consumed stoichiometrically and regulate the tumor redox microenvironment [107]. The catalytic behavior of g-\(C_{2}N_{4}\)-based nanozymes can arise from intrinsic nitrogen-rich sites, structural defects, heteroatom incorporation, or the introduction of redox-active metal centers.
